mainTopic: The power of תפילה, the hope of כנסת ישראל, and preparing for and not interrupting תפילה
overview: רבי אלעזר opens with a series of comparisons: תְּפִלָּה is greater than good deeds and sacrifices, and תַּעֲנִית is greater than צְדָקָה. Along the way, רבי יוחנן rules that a כֹּהֵן who has killed may not give ברכת כהנים. רבי אלעזר then teaches that since the חורבן the gates of prayer are locked, but the gates of tears are always open. The גמרא praises long prayer, then limits that praise to someone who does not count on an answer as guaranteed. It adds that one should pray again when unanswered, and that four things need constant strengthening. An אגדה follows in which כנסת ישראל feels forgotten, and ה׳ promises to forget the עגל but never סיני. The גמרא then returns to the משנה: the early חסידים waited an hour before and after תפילה, and the גמרא explains why one may not interrupt even for a king, except when there is danger. The amud ends with a story of a חסיד who did not answer an official's greeting, and his answer continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Prayer accomplishes what good deeds alone did not
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר points to משה רבינו: despite his exceptional good deeds, he received a limited response through תְּפִלָּה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר says that תְּפִלָּה is greater than good deeds. Even משה רבינו, who excelled in good deeds, received a response only through תְּפִלָּה: the command to stop speaking is followed by permission to climb the mountain.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אלעזר makes a comparison and supports it with what happened to משה רבינו. The two quoted commands show a limited response to his תְּפִלָּה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse does not say that משה רבינו was allowed to enter the land. It shows that after being told to stop asking, he was told to climb and look from the summit.

keyTerms.meaning: next to it in the text

steps.confusionAlert: Being told to climb the mountain is not permission to enter the land; it is the limited response described here.

phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar said:
Prayer is greater than good deeds,
for you have no one greater in good deeds
than Moses our teacher,
nevertheless,
he received a response only through prayer.
As it is stated: “Do not continue speaking to Me,”
and next to it: “Go up to the top of the summit.”

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens this passage with a teaching and its textual support.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: תְּפִלָּה brought משה רבינו a limited response that his good deeds alone had not brought.

steps.title: Fasting involves the person’s body
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר ranks תַּעֲנִית above צְדָקָה because the first involves one’s body and the second one’s money.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר says a fast is greater than charity. Why? This one is done with the body, while that one is done with money.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אלעזר gives another comparison. He immediately asks for the reason and answers it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here, “this one” means תַּעֲנִית, and “that one” means צְדָקָה. The distinction is what a person puts into the act: their body or their money.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Elazar said:
A fast is greater than charity.
What is the reason?
This one is with his body, and that one is with his money.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a separate comparison, with its own question and answer.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: תַּעֲנִית is ranked above צְדָקָה here because it involves the person’s body.

steps.title: Prayer is compared with sacrifices
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר ranks תְּפִלָּה above קָרְבָּנוֹת and points to verses that move from sacrifices to outstretched hands.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר says prayer is greater than sacrifices. The text first says, “Why do I need your many sacrifices?” and later says, “When you spread out your hands.”
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אלעזר returns to תְּפִלָּה, this time comparing it with קָרְבָּנוֹת. He sets two parts of the passage beside each other to support the comparison.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The passage first says ה׳ rejects Israel's sacrifices. A few verses later it adds that even their outstretched hands in prayer will not be heard. The rebuke builds from sacrifices to prayer, which shows that prayer is the higher level of worship. The next step uses the later words of that verse for a different point.

keyTerms.meaning: and when you spread out your hands

phrases.english: And Rabbi Elazar said:
Prayer is greater than sacrifices,
as it is stated, “Why do I need your many sacrifices?”
and it is written, “And when you spread out your hands.”

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר: גְּדוֹלָה תְּפִלָּה יוֹתֵר מִן הַקָּרְבָּנוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins another comparison by רבי אלעזר, now returning to תְּפִלָּה.

steps.title: A priest who has killed may not raise his hands
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן uses the verse’s words about bloodstained hands to prohibit a כֹּהֵן who killed someone from raising his hands.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן says: Any priest who killed a person must not raise his hands, as it is stated, “Your hands are full of blood.”
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן draws a new rule from the passage just quoted. The shared image of raised hands connects this rule to the preceding discussion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The previous step used the passage to discuss תְּפִלָּה. Here, the words about hands full of blood are applied to a כֹּהֵן who killed someone and would otherwise raise his hands for the priestly blessing.

keyTerms.meaning: your hands are full of blood

steps.whatToRemember: The discussion shifts from comparing forms of worship to a rule about who may raise his hands: a כֹּהֵן who has killed may not do so.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yoḥanan said:
Any priest who killed a person—
must not raise his hands,
as it is stated: “Your hands are full of blood.”

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: כׇּל כֹּהֵן שֶׁהָרַג אֶת הַנֶּפֶשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses another part of the verse invoked in step 3 to introduce a new rule.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A כֹּהֵן who killed a person may not raise his hands.

steps.title: Since the חורבן, the gates of prayer are locked
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר teaches that since the חורבן, prayer is not accepted as easily as before. He proves it from a verse in איכה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר also said: From the day the בית המקדש was destroyed, the gates of prayer were locked, as it says: 'Even when I cry out and plead, He shuts out my prayer.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אלעזר gives another teaching about prayer. He says prayer lost some of its power once the בית המקדש was destroyed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse comes from איכה, the book that mourns the חורבן. The speaker cries out, yet his prayer is 'shut out.' רבי אלעזר reads this as describing how prayer works in the time after the חורבן.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Elazar said:
From the day the Temple was destroyed
the gates of prayer were locked,
as it is said: 'Even when I cry out and plead,'
'He shuts out my prayer.'

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר: מִיּוֹם שֶׁחָרַב בֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another teaching of רבי אלעזר about prayer, continuing his series from Steps 1–3.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Since the חורבן, the gates of prayer are locked, based on איכה ג:ח.

steps.title: But the gates of tears were never locked
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר continues: even though the gates of prayer are locked, prayer said with tears still gets through. He proves it from תהלים.
steps.simpleTranslation: And even though the gates of prayer were locked, the gates of tears were not locked, as it says: 'Hear my prayer, ה׳, and listen to my cry; do not be silent at my tears.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אלעזר finishes his statement with an important exception. Prayer with tears still reaches ה׳.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This limits the harsh statement in Step 5. Prayer in general is 'locked,' but tears are an open door. The verse asks ה׳ not to be silent 'at my tears,' which shows that tears get a special hearing.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is a well-known source for the special power of heartfelt, tearful prayer, even in גלות.

phrases.aramaic: וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁשַּׁעֲרֵי תְפִילָּה נִנְעֲלוּ,
phrases.english: And even though the gates of prayer were locked,
the gates of tears were not locked,
as it is said: 'Hear my prayer, Lord,'
'and give ear to my pleading;'
'do not keep silent at my tears.'

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁשַּׁעֲרֵי תְפִילָּה נִנְעֲלוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Same statement of רבי אלעזר. It adds an exception to the locked gates of Step 5.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Tearful prayer is still accepted even after the חורבן.

steps.title: רבא would not decree a fast on a cloudy day
steps.stepSummary: רבא avoided declaring a public fast on a cloudy day, because a verse describes ה׳ covering Himself with a cloud so that prayer cannot pass through.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא did not decree a fast on a cloudy day, because it says: 'You covered Yourself with a cloud, so that prayer cannot pass through.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a related practice of רבא about blocked prayer. A cloudy day was seen as a sign that prayer would not get through, so a fast day of prayer would be less effective.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This connects to the idea of 'locked gates' in Step 5. The verse is also from איכה, and it pictures a cloud blocking prayer. רבא applied it practically: a fast is a day of prayer, so he did not schedule one when the sky signaled that prayer was blocked.

keyTerms.meaning: You covered Yourself with a cloud

phrases.english: Rava did not decree a fast
on a cloudy day,
because it is said:
'You have covered Yourself with a cloud'
'so that prayer cannot pass through.'

steps.triggerLanguage: רָבָא לָא גְּזַר תַּעֲנִיתָא בְּיוֹמָא דְעֵיבָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A practical application of the theme of blocked prayer from Step 5.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Do not decree a public fast on a cloudy day, because clouds signal that prayer is blocked.

steps.title: An iron wall now separates Israel from their Father in Heaven
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר teaches that since the חורבן, an iron wall stands between ישראל and ה׳. He proves it from a symbolic act ה׳ commanded יחזקאל to perform.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי אלעזר said: From the day the בית המקדש was destroyed, an iron wall has separated ישראל from their Father in Heaven, as it says: 'Take for yourself an iron griddle and set it as an iron wall between you and the city.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אלעזר gives a third teaching about the distance created by the חורבן. He describes it as an iron wall between us and ה׳.
steps.deeperAnalysis: ה׳ told יחזקאל to place an iron pan between himself and the city as a sign for ישראל. רבי אלעזר reads this as a picture of the barrier that now stands between ישראל and ה׳. It strengthens the message of Step 5 with a more vivid image.

keyTerms.meaning: Was set up as a separation (here, a dividing barrier)

steps.confusionAlert: Do not read נִפְסְקָה as 'the iron wall stopped.' Here it means the wall came between and separated them, as the verse in יחזקאל shows.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Elazar said:
From the day the Temple was destroyed
an iron wall has separated
between Israel and their Father in Heaven,
as it is said: 'And you, take for yourself an iron griddle'
'and set it as an iron wall'
'between yourself and the city.'

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר: מִיּוֹם שֶׁחָרַב בֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ נִפְסְקָה חוֹמַת בַּרְזֶל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A parallel teaching of רבי אלעזר that also describes the distance created by the חורבן, using a new image.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Since the חורבן, an iron barrier separates ישראל from ה׳, based on יחזקאל ד:ג.

steps.title: Lengthy prayer does not return empty
steps.stepSummary: רבי חנין, quoting רבי חנינא, teaches that someone who prays at length will not have his prayer go unanswered.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חנין said in the name of רבי חנינא: Whoever prays at length, his prayer does not come back empty.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a hopeful teaching about prayer. Praying at length brings results.
steps.deeperAnalysis: After the steps about locked gates and iron walls, this offers encouragement. Persistence and length in prayer help it be accepted. The source for this rule comes in the next step.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי חָנִין אָמַר רַבִּי חֲנִינָא:
phrases.english: Rabbi Ḥanin said that Rabbi Ḥanina said:
Anyone who prolongs his prayer,
his prayer does not return empty.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי חָנִין אָמַר רַבִּי חֲנִינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shifts from the limits of prayer after the חורבן to the power of lengthy prayer.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Lengthy prayer is assured of a response.

steps.title: Proof from משה's long prayer
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the source and proves it from משה רבינו. He prayed for forty days, and right afterward the תורה says ה׳ listened to him.
steps.simpleTranslation: How do we know this? From משה רבינו, as it says: 'And I prayed to ה׳,' and it is written afterward: 'And ה׳ listened to me that time as well.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks 'where do we learn this from?' and answers with a proof from משה רבינו.
steps.deeperAnalysis: משה prayed for forty days and forty nights, which is the ultimate long prayer. The verse that follows says ה׳ listened to him. This shows that lengthy prayer was answered.

keyTerms.meaning: From where do we know this?
And it is written after it

steps.whatToRemember: Prayer has limits after the חורבן: its gates are locked and an iron wall separates us from ה׳. Still, tears always get through, and long, persistent prayer like משה's does not go unanswered. Step 13 adds a limit: this holds when the person does not count on an answer as guaranteed.

phrases.english: From where do we know this? From Moses our teacher,
as it is said: 'And I prayed to the Lord,'
phrases.notes: דברים ט:כו, after forty days of prayer

phrases.english: and it is written after it:
'And the Lord listened to me that time as well.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the scriptural source for רבי חנינא's rule in Step 9.
steps.raayaObject: That lengthy prayer does not return unanswered.
steps.raayaSupportSource: משה's forty days of prayer (דברים ט:כו), followed by 'וַיִּשְׁמַע ה׳ אֵלַי' (דברים י:י).

steps.title: A warning about lengthy prayer
steps.stepSummary: A teaching from רבי יוחנן seems to contradict the earlier praise of praying at length.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is that so? רבי חייא בר אבא said in the name of רבי יוחנן: Someone who prays at length and expects an answer will eventually suffer heartache, as the verse says, “Hope deferred makes the heart sick.”
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the teaching in steps 9–10. It brings a warning that lengthy prayer can lead to heartache.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The warning includes a second action: the person examines the prayer expectantly, looking for an answer. That detail will allow the גמרא to distinguish this case from the earlier teaching.

keyTerms.meaning: looks expectantly for the prayer to be answered

phrases.aramaic: אִינִי?! וְהָא אָמַר רַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אַבָּא
phrases.english: Is that so?! But Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba said

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: כָּל הַמַּאֲרִיךְ בִּתְפִילָּתוֹ
phrases.english: that Rabbi Yoḥanan said: Anyone who prolongs his prayer

phrases.aramaic: וּמְעַיֵּין בָּהּ — סוֹף בָּא לִידֵי כְּאֵב לֵב,
phrases.english: and expects an answer to it will ultimately come to heartache,
as it is stated: “Hope deferred makes the heart sick.”

steps.triggerLanguage: אִינִי?! וְהָא אָמַר רַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אַבָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the proof that praying at length is beneficial.
steps.kashyaTarget: The teaching in steps 9–10 that a person who prays at length will not have the prayer go unanswered.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי יוחנן describes a person who prays at length and looks expectantly for an answer as someone who will suffer heartache.

steps.title: A remedy for the heartache
steps.stepSummary: The quoted teaching asks what helps someone with this heartache and answers: engaging in תורה.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the remedy? The person should engage in תורה. The verse speaks of a “tree of life,” and another verse uses that description for תורה.
steps.whatsHappening: The quoted teaching now gives a remedy for the heartache it described. It supports that remedy by connecting two verses through the words “tree of life.”
steps.deeperAnalysis: This answers what the person should do after the pain arises. It does not yet answer the גמרא’s challenge about lengthy prayer; that comes next.

phrases.english: What is his remedy? He should engage in Torah,
as it is stated: “But desire fulfilled is a tree of life,”
and “tree of life” means Torah,
as it is stated: “It is a tree of life to those who hold fast to it.”

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the quoted teaching by giving a remedy for its heartache.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What should someone suffering this heartache do?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Engage in תורה, which the second verse calls a tree of life.

steps.title: Length is not the problem by itself
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא separates lengthy prayer with an expectation of an answer from lengthy prayer without that expectation.
steps.simpleTranslation: There is no difficulty: One teaching concerns someone who prays at length and expects an answer; the other concerns someone who prays at length and does not expect an answer.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא resolves the apparent contradiction. It says the two teachings describe different ways of praying at length.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier praise applies when the person prays at length without treating an answer as guaranteed. רבי יוחנן’s warning applies when the person also waits expectantly for a result.
steps.whatToRemember: The distinction is not whether the prayer is long. It is whether the person expects an answer as a sure result.

keyTerms.meaning: and does not look expectantly for an answer

phrases.aramaic: לָא קַשְׁיָא, הָא דְּמַאֲרֵיךְ וּמְעַיֵּין בַּהּ.
phrases.english: There is no difficulty: This concerns one who prolongs prayer and expects an answer.
That concerns one who prolongs prayer and does not expect an answer.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא קַשְׁיָא, הָא דְּמַאֲרֵיךְ וּמְעַיֵּין בַּהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns from the remedy to resolve the challenge raised in step 11.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishes two cases by whether the person expects an answer.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The praise and warning both seemed to apply to anyone who prays at length.
steps.terutzMaskana: The warning applies to lengthy prayer with expectant scrutiny; the praise applies to lengthy prayer without it.

steps.title: Pray again when no answer is seen
steps.stepSummary: רבי חמא ברבי חנינא teaches that someone who has prayed without seeing an answer should pray again.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חמא ברבי חנינא said: If a person prayed and was not answered, that person should pray again. The verse says to hope in ה׳, take courage, and hope in ה׳ again.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a related teaching about what to do when prayer appears unanswered. רבי חמא ברבי חנינא says to pray again.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse says “hope” twice, with encouragement between the two calls. The teaching reads that pattern as support for returning to prayer rather than giving up.

keyTerms.meaning: he should return and pray again

phrases.english: Rabbi Ḥama, son of Rabbi Ḥanina, said:

phrases.aramaic: אִם רָאָה אָדָם שֶׁהִתְפַּלֵּל וְלֹא נַעֲנָה
phrases.english: If a person saw that he prayed and was not answered,
he should return and pray again, as it is stated:

phrases.aramaic: ״קַוֵּה אֶל ה׳ חֲזַק וְיַאֲמֵץ לִבֶּךָ וְקַוֵּה אֶל ה׳״.
phrases.english: “Hope in the Lord; be strong and let your heart take courage; and hope in the Lord.”

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After distinguishing healthy persistence from harmful expectation, introduces a teaching that encourages praying again.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If a person prayed and did not see an answer, the person should pray again.

steps.title: Four areas need continued strength
steps.stepSummary: A teaching of the חכמים lists four areas that require sustained effort.
steps.simpleTranslation: The חכמים taught: Four things need strengthening—תורה, good deeds, prayer, and everyday occupation.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא broadens the theme of persistence beyond prayer. It introduces a list of four areas that need continued strengthening.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Prayer is one item on the list, connecting this teaching to the instruction to pray again. The list sets up the next move: finding support for its items in verses.

phrases.english: The Sages taught: Four things require strengthening,
and these are they: Torah and good deeds,
prayer and everyday occupation.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Expands the idea of persistence in prayer into a four-part teaching.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: תורה, good deeds, prayer, and דֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ all require continued effort.

steps.title: A verse supports strength in learning and deeds
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for support for the first two items and reads two calls for strength as applying to תורה and good deeds.
steps.simpleTranslation: From where do we know this about תורה and good deeds? The verse says, “Only be strong and very courageous, to observe and do all the תורה.” “Be strong” refers to תורה; “be courageous” refers to good deeds.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for a source for the first two items in the list and immediately supplies one. It assigns the verse’s two calls for strength to תורה and good deeds.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse joins “be strong” and “be courageous” with observing and doing the תורה. The גמרא uses the two expressions to support continued effort in both learning and action.

phrases.english: From where is this known about Torah and good deeds? As it is stated:
“Only be strong and very courageous, to observe and do
all the Torah”; “be strong” refers to Torah,
and “be courageous” refers to good deeds.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins supplying verse-based support for the four-part list, starting with תורה and good deeds.
steps.raayaObject: The claim that תורה and good deeds require strengthening.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The verse commanding “חֲזַק וֶאֱמַץ” in connection with observing and doing the תורה.

steps.title: Proof that prayer needs strengthening
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a פסוק showing that תפלה needs constant effort and renewed strength.
steps.simpleTranslation: Where do we learn that prayer needs strengthening? As it says: 'Hope in ה׳, be strong and let your heart take courage, and hope in ה׳.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא continues its list of sources and now proves the third item, תפלה. It quotes a פסוק that says 'hope in ה׳' twice, with 'be strong' in the middle.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק says 'hope in ה׳', then 'be strong', then 'hope in ה׳' again. This shows that if your first prayer was not answered, you should strengthen yourself and pray again. It fits the earlier teaching of רבי חמא ברבי חנינא from Step 14.

keyTerms.meaning: From where do we know? (asking for a source)

phrases.english: Prayer, from where do we know it needs strengthening?
As it says: 'Hope in the Lord,'
be strong and let your heart take courage,
and hope in the Lord.'
phrases.notes: The repeated 'hope' teaches that one should pray again.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the source list from Step 16 and moves to the third item.
steps.raayaSupportSource: תהלים כז:יד, 'קוה אל ה׳ חזק ויאמץ לבך וקוה אל ה׳'

steps.title: Proof that one's livelihood needs strengthening
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a פסוק showing that דרך ארץ (a person's work and occupation) needs strength.
steps.simpleTranslation: Where do we learn that one's occupation needs strengthening? As it says: 'Be strong and let us strengthen ourselves for our nation, etc.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא proves the fourth and last item on the list, דרך ארץ. Here that means a person's work or occupation. This finishes the list of four.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the פסוק, יואב speaks to his brother אבישי before battle. A soldier's task is his 'job', so the פסוק is read as teaching that every kind of work needs effort and renewed strength.

keyTerms.meaning: Here: worldly occupation, earning a living

steps.whatToRemember: Four things need constant strengthening: תורה, good deeds, תפלה, and דרך ארץ. Each one has its own פסוק.
steps.confusionAlert: Here דרך ארץ does not mean 'good manners'. In this context it means a person's work or livelihood.

phrases.english: Occupation, from where do we know it needs strengthening?
As it says: 'Be strong and let us strengthen ourselves'
for the sake of our nation, etc.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the last source and completes the list of four.
steps.raayaObject: That דרך ארץ (one's occupation) needs sustained strengthening.
steps.raayaSupportSource: שמואל ב י:יב, 'חזק ונתחזק בעד עמנו'

steps.title: Why does the verse say both forsaken and forgotten?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a פסוק from ישעיה and asks why it uses two words that seem to mean the same thing.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And Zion said: ה׳ has forsaken me, and ה׳ has forgotten me.' Isn't 'forsaken' the same as 'forgotten'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a new topic. It quotes a פסוק and asks a wording question: why use two words when one would do? This sets up ריש לקיש's answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The assumption is that every word of a פסוק adds something. If 'forsaken' and 'forgotten' mean the same thing, one of them seems extra. So the גמרא looks for a difference between them.

keyTerms.meaning: Zion: stands for the Jewish people

phrases.english: 'And Zion said: The Lord has forsaken me,'
'and the Lord has forgotten me.'
Isn't 'forsaken' the same as 'forgotten'?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to a new אגדה about the relationship between ה׳ and Israel.

steps.title: Israel's complaint: more than left, also forgotten
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש explains that כנסת ישראל complained that ה׳ had not only left her but also forgotten her. Even a man who takes a second wife still remembers his first wife.
steps.simpleTranslation: ריש לקיש said: כנסת ישראל said before the הקדוש ברוך הוא: Master of the world, even a man who marries a second wife after his first still remembers what his first wife did. But You have both forsaken me and forgotten me.
steps.whatsHappening: ריש לקיש answers the question from Step 19. The two words describe two different hurts: being left, and also being forgotten.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Forsaken' means ה׳ turned to someone else, like a man taking another wife. 'Forgotten' is worse: even such a husband still remembers his first wife's good deeds. Israel complains that ה׳ did not even remember her.

keyTerms.meaning: The community of Israel (pictured as a wife)
The deeds of the first wife

phrases.english: Reish Lakish said:
The community of Israel said
before the Holy One, Blessed be He:
Master of the world,

phrases.aramaic: אָדָם נוֹשֵׂא אִשָּׁה עַל אִשְׁתּוֹ רִאשׁוֹנָה,
phrases.english: a man who marries a wife in addition to his first wife
still remembers the deeds of the first one.
But You have forsaken me and forgotten me.
phrases.notes: Two separate hurts, which explains the two words.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ: אָמְרָה כְּנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל לִפְנֵי הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the wording question of Step 19.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: 'Forsaken' means ה׳ turned away from Israel. 'Forgotten' adds that ה׳ did not even remember her past deeds, which is worse than how a man treats his first wife.

steps.title: God's answer: the whole heavens were made for you
steps.stepSummary: The הקדוש ברוך הוא answers כנסת ישראל by describing a vast structure of constellations, armies, and countless stars, all created for her sake. So how can she say she was forsaken and forgotten?
steps.simpleTranslation: The הקדוש ברוך הוא said to her: My daughter, I created twelve מזלות in the sky. For each one I made thirty armies, for each army thirty legions, for each legion thirty divisions, for each division thirty camps, and for each camp thirty forts. On each fort I hung 365 thousand myriads of stars, matching the days of the solar year. I created all of them only for you, and you say, 'You forsook me' and 'You forgot me'?!
steps.whatsHappening: The הקדוש ברוך הוא replies to Israel's complaint. He shows her how enormous the heavens are, and that all of it was made only for her.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each level multiplies the one before it by thirty, then by an enormous number of stars. This shows how vast creation is. Since all of it exists for Israel's sake, it proves that ה׳ is always thinking about her, so she has not been forgotten.

keyTerms.meaning: My daughter (a loving way of addressing Israel)
A fort or troop unit (a borrowed word)

steps.whatToRemember: The double wording 'forsaken' and 'forgotten' reflects a double complaint. ה׳ answers it by showing that all of creation exists for Israel, so she could never be forgotten.
steps.whyThisMatters: It continues the theme of not giving up on prayer and hope: even when Israel feels abandoned, ה׳'s care is constant.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לָהּ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא: בִּתִּי,
phrases.english: The Holy One, Blessed be He, said to her: My daughter,
I created twelve constellations in the sky,
and for each and every constellation
I created thirty armies,
and for each and every army
I created thirty legions,
and for each and every legion
I created thirty infantry divisions,
and for each and every division
I created thirty camps,
and for each and every camp
I created thirty forts,
and on each and every fort

phrases.aramaic: תָּלִיתִי בּוֹ שְׁלֹשׁ מֵאוֹת וְשִׁשִּׁים וַחֲמִשָּׁה
phrases.english: I hung three hundred sixty-five
thousands of myriads of stars
corresponding to the days of the solar year.
And I created all of them only for your sake,
and you say 'You have forsaken me' and 'You have forgotten me'?!
phrases.notes: A rhetorical question that rejects Israel's complaint.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לָהּ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא: בִּתִּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: ה׳'s reply rejects the complaint that ריש לקיש described in Step 20.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: All of creation was made for Israel's sake, so Israel is neither forsaken nor forgotten.

steps.title: God will not forget Israel's offerings in the desert
steps.stepSummary: The הקדוש ברוך הוא reads ״עולה״ as hinting to עולות (burnt offerings). He tells כנסת ישראל that He will never forget the קרבנות she brought in the מדבר.
steps.simpleTranslation: "Can a woman forget her nursing baby?" The הקדוש ברוך הוא said: Could I ever forget the burnt offerings of rams and the firstborn animals that you brought before Me in the desert?!
steps.whatsHappening: ה׳ continues answering כנסת ישראל's complaint from the previous step. He uses the next פסוק to show that He remembers every קרבן she ever brought.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word עוּלָהּ (her nursing baby) sounds like עוֹלוֹת (burnt offerings), so the גמרא reads it as a hint to Israel's קרבנות. In the same way, ״מֵרַחֵם בֶּן בִּטְנָהּ״ in the פסוק is linked to פטרי רחמים, the firstborn animals that open the womb (רֶחֶם). A mother never forgets her baby, and ה׳ never forgets Israel's devotion.

keyTerms.meaning: Her nursing baby. Here it is read as a hint to עוֹלוֹת (burnt offerings).
Firstborn animals, literally 'those that open the womb'
Could it be that...? A word that sets up a rhetorical question

phrases.english: "Can a woman forget her nursing baby?"
phrases.notes: ישעיה מט:טו, the continuation of the פסוק from earlier steps.

phrases.english: The Holy One, Blessed be He, said:
Could I ever forget the burnt offerings of rams
phrases.notes: Wordplay: עוּלָהּ is read as עוֹלוֹת.

phrases.english: and the firstborn animals
that you offered before Me in the desert?!

steps.triggerLanguage: ״הֲתִשְׁכַּח אִשָּׁה עוּלָהּ״, אָמַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues ה׳'s reply to כנסת ישראל's complaint of being forgotten.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: ה׳ never forgets the קרבנות Israel brought in the מדבר.

steps.title: Israel worries that the חטא העגל will also be remembered
steps.stepSummary: כנסת ישראל asks: if ה׳ never forgets anything, will He also never forget the sin of the עגל?
steps.simpleTranslation: She said before Him: Master of the World, since there is no forgetting before Your Throne of Glory, perhaps You will not forget the sin of the Golden Calf for me?
steps.whatsHappening: כנסת ישראל turns ה׳'s comfort into a worry. Perfect memory sounds good, but it means her sins would be remembered too. This question sets up ה׳'s answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The logic is simple: if nothing is forgotten, then the bad is remembered along with the good. So the promise 'I remember your offerings' seems to carry a frightening side effect, the memory of the עגל.

keyTerms.meaning: The sin of the Golden Calf

phrases.english: She said before Him:
Master of the World,
since there is no forgetting
before Your Throne of Glory,

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁמָּא לֹא תִּשְׁכַּח לִי מַעֲשֵׂה הָעֵגֶל?
phrases.english: perhaps You will not forget for me the sin of the Calf?

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרָה לְפָנָיו: רִבּוֹנוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם, הוֹאִיל וְאֵין שִׁכְחָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Raises a worry that follows from ה׳'s claim of perfect memory.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Will ה׳'s perfect memory also preserve the sin of the עגל?

steps.title: The Golden Calf will be forgotten
steps.stepSummary: ה׳ answers with the פסוק ״גם אלה תשכחנה״. ״אלה״ (these) hints to the עגל, which will be forgotten.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to her: "These, too, will be forgotten."
steps.whatsHappening: ה׳ reassures כנסת ישראל that the sin of the עגל will be forgotten, using the next words of the פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word אֵלֶּה links to what the people said at the עגל: ״אלה אלהיך ישראל״ (these are your gods, Israel). So ״גם אלה תשכחנה״ is read as 'even the sin of אלה will be forgotten.'

keyTerms.meaning: These. A hint to ״אלה אלהיך ישראל״, said at the עגל

phrases.english: He said to her:
"These, too, will be forgotten."
phrases.notes: ״אלה״ points to the עגל: ״אלה אלהיך ישראל״.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the worry about the עגל.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The sin of the עגל (״אלה״) will be forgotten.

steps.title: Israel worries that סיני might also be forgotten
steps.stepSummary: כנסת ישראל asks: if ה׳ can forget, might He also forget מעמד הר סיני and her acceptance of the Torah?
steps.simpleTranslation: She said before Him: Master of the World, since there is forgetting before Your Throne of Glory, perhaps You will forget the events of Sinai for me?
steps.whatsHappening: Now כנסת ישראל worries from the opposite side. If ה׳ forgets, maybe He will forget her greatest merit too. This question sets up ה׳'s final answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each answer seems to raise a new risk. Perfect memory threatens to keep her sin alive. Forgetting threatens to erase her merit. כנסת ישראל needs to hear that forgetting works only one way.

keyTerms.meaning: The events at Sinai, meaning the receiving of the Torah

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a contradiction about whether ה׳ forgets. The point of the story is that ה׳ chooses to forget Israel's sins but never forgets her good deeds.

phrases.english: She said before Him: Master of the World,

phrases.aramaic: הוֹאִיל וְיֵשׁ שִׁכְחָה לִפְנֵי כִּסֵּא כְבוֹדֶךָ,
phrases.english: since there is forgetting before Your Throne of Glory,
perhaps You will forget for me the events of Sinai?

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרָה לְפָנָיו: רִבּוֹנוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם, הוֹאִיל וְיֵשׁ שִׁכְחָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Flips the logic of the answer just given and raises the opposite worry.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: If ה׳ can forget, will He forget the merit of סיני?

steps.title: סיני will never be forgotten
steps.stepSummary: ה׳ answers with ״ואנכי לא אשכחך״. ״אנכי״ hints to the first word of the עשרת הדברות, so סיני will never be forgotten.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to her: "But I (אנכי) will not forget you."
steps.whatsHappening: ה׳ promises that the merit of receiving the Torah at סיני will never be forgotten.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אָנֹכִי is the first word of the עשרת הדברות: ״אנכי ה׳ אלהיך״. So the פסוק is read as 'the אנכי of סיני I will not forget.' Read together with the previous step, the sin is forgotten and the merit is remembered forever.

keyTerms.meaning: "I". A hint to ״אנכי ה׳ אלהיך״ at סיני

steps.whatToRemember: ה׳ forgets Israel's sin (the עגל, ״אלה״) and never forgets her merit (סיני, ״אנכי״).

phrases.english: He said to her: "But I will not forget you."
phrases.notes: ״אנכי״ points to ״אנכי ה׳ אלהיך״ at סיני.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the worry about סיני and closes the dialogue.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The merit of סיני (״אנכי״) will never be forgotten.

steps.title: רב אושעיא's teaching matches this reading
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא shows that this reading matches what רבי אלעזר taught in the name of רב אושעיא: ״גם אלה תשכחנה״ refers to the עגל, and ״ואנכי לא אשכחך״ refers to סיני.
steps.simpleTranslation: And this is what רבי אלעזר said in the name of רב אושעיא: What is the meaning of the פסוק "These, too, will be forgotten"? That is the sin of the Calf. "But I will not forget you"? That is the events of Sinai.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings an earlier teaching that backs up the reading it just gave.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase ״והיינו דאמר״ ('and this is what so-and-so said') shows that the story matches an established interpretation. This confirms that ״אלה״ means the עגל and ״אנכי״ means סיני.

keyTerms.meaning: And this is what so-and-so said. Introduces a teaching that matches what was just said
An אמורא who reports the teaching
The אמורא who is the source of the teaching
What is the meaning of what is written

phrases.english: And this is what Rabbi Elazar said
in the name of Rav Oshaya:
What is the meaning of what is written, "These, too, will be forgotten"?
That is the sin of the Calf;
"But I will not forget you":
That is the events of Sinai.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהַיְינוּ דְּאָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר אָמַר רַב אוֹשַׁעְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the readings given in steps 24 and 26.
steps.raayaObject: Reading ״אלה״ as the עגל and ״אנכי״ as סיני
steps.raayaSupportSource: The teaching of רבי אלעזר in the name of רב אושעיא

steps.title: Back to the משנה: the early pious men waited an hour
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא returns to the משנה and quotes its next line: the חסידים הראשונים would wait one hour before praying.
steps.simpleTranslation: The early pious men would wait one hour before praying.
steps.whatsHappening: The אגדה is finished, and the גמרא goes back to the משנה. It quotes the line about the early חסידים to set up a new discussion of it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a quote from the משנה, not a new statement. It opens a new section that will explain why these חסידים waited before תפלה and where that practice comes from.

keyTerms.meaning: One hour (or a period of time)

phrases.english: The early pious men
would wait one hour.
phrases.notes: They waited before תפלה to prepare their minds.

steps.triggerLanguage: חֲסִידִים הָרִאשׁוֹנִים הָיוּ שׁוֹהִין שָׁעָה אַחַת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the אגדה and returns to the next line of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The early חסידים waited one hour before praying.

steps.title: What is the source for waiting before prayer?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the source of the משנה's practice of waiting one hour before praying.
steps.simpleTranslation: From where do we learn these things?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks where the חסידים הראשונים got the idea of waiting before תפילה. This question sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה only described what the חסידים הראשונים did. Now the גמרא wants a פסוק that supports the practice, so it is not just a personal custom.

keyTerms.meaning: From where are these words (learned)? A standard request for a source

phrases.english: From where are these matters derived?
phrases.notes: Refers to the משנה's line about waiting one hour before praying

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source of the משנה line quoted in Step 28
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A פסוק that supports waiting one hour before תפילה

steps.title: Waiting before prayer comes from 'Happy are those who dwell in Your House'
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע בן לוי brings the פסוק ״אשרי יושבי ביתך״ as the source for waiting before prayer.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהושע בן לוי said: the verse says, "Happy are those who dwell in Your House."
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע בן לוי answers the question with a פסוק from תהלים. The verse praises people who sit in ה׳'s house.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse first praises those who 'sit' in ה׳'s house. Only afterward does it say 'they will praise You.' So the sitting and waiting comes first, and the praising, which is prayer, comes after.

keyTerms.meaning: Happy are those who dwell in Your House (תהלים פד:ה)

steps.confusionAlert: The proof depends on the end of the פסוק, which the גמרא does not quote: ״עוד יהללוך סלה״. First comes the sitting, and then the praise.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said:
The verse states: "Happy are those who dwell in Your House."
phrases.notes: The verse continues: 'they will yet praise You.' Sitting comes before praising.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן לֵוִי, אָמַר קְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in Step 29
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: ״אשרי יושבי ביתך״: sitting in ה׳'s house comes before praising Him

steps.title: One must also wait an hour after praying
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע בן לוי adds that a person should also wait an hour after תפילה, based on ״אך צדיקים יודו לשמך ישבו ישרים את פניך״.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יהושע בן לוי said: one who prays must wait one hour after his prayer, as it says, "Surely the righteous will thank Your name; the upright will sit before You."
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע בן לוי adds a new rule. Besides waiting before תפילה, a person should also wait after it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this verse the order is reversed. First the righteous 'thank Your name', which is the prayer. Then 'the upright will sit before You', which is the waiting. So the waiting comes after praying.

keyTerms.meaning: The upright will sit before You (תהלים קמ:יד)

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said:
One who prays must wait
one hour after his prayer,
as it is stated: "Surely the righteous will give thanks to Your name,
the upright will sit before You."
phrases.notes: Sitting is the waiting that comes afterward

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second statement by the same אמורא, adding waiting after תפילה
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A person who prays should wait one hour after his תפילה

steps.title: A ברייתא supports both sources
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that one should wait an hour before and an hour after prayer, using the same two פסוקים.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was also taught this way in a ברייתא: one who prays must wait one hour before his prayer and one hour after his prayer. From where do we learn 'before his prayer'? As it says, "Happy are those who dwell in Your House." From where do we learn 'after his prayer'? As it is written, "Surely the righteous will thank Your name; the upright will sit before You."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that a ברייתא says exactly what רבי יהושע בן לוי said. Both of his teachings now have support from a תנאי source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase תניא נמי הכי means 'it was also taught like this.' Its job is to confirm the אמורא's teaching. The ברייתא uses the same two פסוקים: one for waiting before prayer and one for waiting after it.

keyTerms.meaning: It was also taught this way (a ברייתא supports the statement)

phrases.english: It was also taught this way:
One who prays must wait
one hour before his prayer,
and one hour after his prayer.
Before his prayer, from where do we know?
As it is stated: "Happy are those who dwell in Your House."
After his prayer, from where do we know?
As it is written: "Surely the righteous will give thanks to Your name,
the upright will sit before You."

steps.whatToRemember: Waiting before תפילה comes from ״אשרי יושבי ביתך״. Waiting after תפילה comes from ״ישבו ישרים את פניך״. Both are taught by רבי יהושע בן לוי and confirmed by a ברייתא.
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports Steps 30 and 31 with a ברייתא
steps.raayaObject: רבי יהושע בן לוי's two teachings about waiting before and after תפילה
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא that teaches both rules with the same פסוקים

steps.title: The early pious ones waited, prayed, and waited again
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא describes the חסידים הראשונים: an hour of waiting, an hour of prayer, and another hour of waiting.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: the early pious ones would wait one hour, pray for one hour, and then wait one more hour.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another ברייתא describing how the חסידים הראשונים actually prayed. This step sets up the question that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the prayer itself also lasts a full hour. So each תפילה takes three hours in total. That number becomes the basis of the next question.

keyTerms.meaning: And they go back (do it again)

phrases.english: The Sages taught:

phrases.aramaic: חֲסִידִים הָרִאשׁוֹנִים הָיוּ שׁוֹהִין שָׁעָה אַחַת,
phrases.english: The early pious ones would wait one hour,
and pray for one hour,
and then wait one hour again.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a fuller description of the חסידים הראשונים's practice
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The חסידים הראשונים spent three hours on each תפילה: waiting, praying, and waiting again

steps.title: How did they have time for Torah and work?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: if they spent nine hours a day on prayer, how did they keep their Torah learning and get their work done?
steps.simpleTranslation: But since they spent nine hours a day on prayer, how was their Torah preserved, and how was their work done?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the practice. It seems impossible to spend so much of the day on prayer and still keep up Torah learning and earn a living.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Three תפילות a day, at three hours each, adds up to nine hours. With so little time left, the גמרא asks how they reviewed their learning and did their work. The next step answers this.
steps.confusionAlert: Where does 'nine hours' come from? It is 3 תפילות × 3 hours each (wait, pray, wait).

phrases.english: But since they spend
nine hours a day in prayer,
how is their Torah preserved?
And how is their work done?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי מֵאַחַר שֶׁשּׁוֹהִין תֵּשַׁע שָׁעוֹת בַּיּוֹם בִּתְפִלָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges whether the practice described in Step 33 is practical
steps.kashyaTarget: The practice of the חסידים הראשונים to spend three hours on each תפילה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Nine hours a day would leave too little time to keep up Torah learning and do one's work

steps.title: Their piety kept their Torah and blessed their work
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that because the חסידים הראשונים were pious, their Torah stayed with them and their work was blessed, even with less time.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, because they were pious, their Torah is preserved and their work is blessed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from Step 34 about how the חסידים found time for learning and work. The answer is that heaven helped them because of their piety.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question assumed that less time means less Torah and less income. The answer rejects that assumption. Their piety brought a ברכה, so their Torah did not fade and their work produced enough even with fewer hours.

keyTerms.meaning: Pious people who go beyond what is required

steps.whatToRemember: The חסידים הראשונים spent about nine hours a day on תפילה. They did not lose Torah or income, because their piety brought a ברכה on both.

phrases.english: Rather, because they are pious ones
phrases.notes: 'אלא' signals the answer to the previous question.

phrases.english: their Torah is preserved,
and their work is blessed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the difficulty raised in Step 34.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rejects the hidden assumption: success depends on ברכה, not only on hours spent.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Nine hours of תפילה each day should leave too little time for Torah and work.
steps.terutzMaskana: Their piety brought a ברכה, so their Torah lasted and their work was enough.

steps.title: The משנה: do not answer even a king's greeting
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the next line of the משנה: a person in the middle of תפילה should not answer even a king who greets him.
steps.simpleTranslation: Even if the king greets him, he should not answer him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא returns to the משנה and quotes its next rule. This is a setup line that prepares for רב יוסף's comment in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה shows how serious it is to stop in the middle of תפילה. Even a king, whom one normally must honor, does not justify an interruption. The next step asks which kings this includes.

keyTerms.meaning: Greets him (literally, asks about his welfare)

phrases.english: Even if the king greets him
he should not answer him.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲפִילּוּ הַמֶּלֶךְ שׁוֹאֵל בִּשְׁלוֹמוֹ לֹא יְשִׁיבֶנּוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves away from the topic of the חסידים to a new line of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Do not interrupt תפילה to answer a king's greeting.

steps.title: רב יוסף: the rule applies only to Jewish kings
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף limits the משנה to Jewish kings. For a non-Jewish king, a person does interrupt his תפילה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף said: They only taught this about kings of Israel. But for kings of the nations of the world, he interrupts.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף explains that the משנה's rule covers only Jewish kings. If a non-Jewish king greets you, you should stop and answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A Jewish king understands why you did not answer, so there is no danger. A non-Jewish king may be offended and could kill you. Because your life is at risk, you interrupt.

keyTerms.meaning: They only taught this about; a phrase that limits a rule
The non-Jewish nations of the world

steps.whyThisMatters: This limit on the משנה becomes the target of the challenge in the next step.

phrases.english: Rav Yosef said:
They only taught this regarding kings of Israel,
but regarding kings of the nations of the world, he interrupts.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יוֹסֵף, לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא לְמַלְכֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Narrows the משנה quoted in Step 36.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Interrupt תפילה to answer a non-Jewish king, because of danger. Do not interrupt for a Jewish king.

steps.title: Challenge: even when danger approaches, one does not interrupt
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says that a person praying who sees a dangerous person or a carriage coming toward him should not stop. He should shorten his תפילה and move away. This seems to contradict רב יוסף.
steps.simpleTranslation: They challenged: One who is praying and saw a violent person coming toward him, or saw a carriage coming toward him, should not stop. Rather, he shortens his prayer and moves out of the way.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב יוסף with a ברייתא. The ברייתא says not to stop praying even when danger is coming.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב יוסף said that danger from a non-Jewish king is a reason to interrupt. Yet the ברייתא faces real danger from a violent person or a carriage, and still says not to interrupt, only to shorten the תפילה. So why should a non-Jewish king's greeting be different?

keyTerms.meaning: They raised an objection from a ברייתא
And moves out of the way

steps.confusionAlert: Here 'ועולה' does not mean 'goes up.' It means he moves out of the way of the danger.

phrases.english: They raised an objection:
One who is praying and saw a violent person coming toward him,
or saw a carriage coming toward him,
he should not stop,
but rather shortens his prayer and moves out of the way!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רב יוסף's statement from Step 37.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב יוסף's rule that one interrupts תפילה for a non-Jewish king.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא does not allow stopping even when there is clear danger. So danger alone should not allow stopping for a non-Jewish king.

steps.title: Shorten if you can, stop if you can't
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא reconciles the ברייתא with רב יוסף: the ברייתא is a case where shortening is possible; if it is not possible, one stops.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is not difficult. The ברייתא is talking about a case where he can shorten his תפילה, so he should shorten it. If he cannot, he stops.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from step 38 by saying the two sources are talking about different situations.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא said "shorten, don't stop." That is when there is enough time to finish a short version before the danger arrives. When there is no time, he must stop, just as רב יוסף said for a non-Jewish king.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not difficult. A formula that opens an answer.

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets a clear order for a person in danger during תפילה: first try to shorten. Only if that is impossible does he stop completely.

phrases.english: It is not difficult.
This is where it is possible to shorten: he should shorten.
phrases.notes: Refers to the ברייתא that said to shorten.

phrases.english: And if not, he stops.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in step 38.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (אוקימתא): each source covers a different situation.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא seemed to say one never stops, even in danger, against רב יוסף.
steps.terutzMaskana: Shorten if there is time. If there is no time, stop.

steps.title: A חסיד keeps praying when an official greets him
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא tells of a חסיד praying on the road who did not return a הגמון's greeting. The official waited until he finished.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: A pious man was praying on the road. An official came and greeted him, and he did not greet him back. The official waited until he finished his תפילה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a story connected to the topic of not interrupting תפילה. This step sets up the scene for the argument that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The חסיד did not stop for a non-Jewish official, even though רב יוסף said one should stop for a non-Jewish king. The story will show how the חסיד defended what he did.

keyTerms.meaning: The Rabbis taught. Introduces a ברייתא.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
There was an incident with a certain pious man
who was praying on the road.
A certain official came
and greeted him,
and he did not return the greeting.
The official waited for him until he finished his prayer.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a story about the same topic as the משנה: not interrupting תפילה for a ruler's greeting.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A חסיד did not interrupt his תפילה to answer a non-Jewish official's greeting.

steps.title: The official scolds the חסיד for risking his life
steps.stepSummary: The official calls the חסיד a fool. He quotes the Torah's command to guard one's life and says he could have killed him with no one to punish him.
steps.simpleTranslation: After he finished, the official said: You empty one! Isn't it written in your Torah, "Only guard yourself and guard your soul," and "Guard yourselves very much"? When I greeted you, why didn't you greet me back? If I had cut off your head with a sword, who would have demanded your blood from me?!
steps.whatsHappening: Inside the story, the official attacks the חסיד's behavior. He says that by ignoring him, the חסיד put his own life in danger.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The official uses the Jews' own Torah against the חסיד. The Torah commands you to protect your life, yet you ignored a powerful ruler who could have killed you. The challenge is: how could your תפילה be worth risking your life?
steps.confusionAlert: Don't get thrown off: the official quotes פסוקים, but he is not a חכם giving a halachic ruling. He is an angry character in the story, and the חסיד is about to answer him.

phrases.english: After he finished his prayer, the official said to him:
You empty one!
Isn't it written in your Torah:
"Only guard yourself and guard your soul diligently"
And it is written: "Guard yourselves very much."
When I greeted you,
why did you not return my greeting?
If I had cut off your head with a sword,

phrases.aramaic: מִי הָיָה תּוֹבֵעַ אֶת דָּמְךָ מִיָּדִי?!
phrases.english: who would have demanded your blood from my hand?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The official responds to the חסיד's refusal described in step 40.
steps.kashyaTarget: The חסיד's choice not to interrupt his תפילה for the official.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The Torah requires guarding one's life, and ignoring a powerful ruler is a deadly risk. So the חסיד seemingly violated the Torah.

steps.title: The חסיד begins his answer with a parable about a human king
steps.stepSummary: The חסיד asks the official to wait while he explains. He begins a parable: if you stood before a human king and a friend greeted you, would you answer?
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Wait until I calm you down with words. He said: If you were standing before a human king, and your friend came and greeted you, would you...
steps.whatsHappening: The חסיד starts to defend himself. He sets up a comparison that is finished on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The חסיד's point is that during תפילה he stands before ה׳, the King of all kings. Just as one would not stop to greet a friend while standing before a human king, he could not stop for the official. The sentence is cut off here and continues on the next amud.

keyTerms.meaning: A human king (literally: of flesh and blood)

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לוֹ: הַמְתֵּן לִי עַד שֶׁאֲפַיֶּיסְךָ בִּדְבָרִים.
phrases.english: The pious man said to him: Wait for me until I appease you with words.
He said to him: If you had been standing
before a flesh-and-blood king,
and your friend came and greeted you,
would you...
phrases.notes: The sentence continues on the next amud: "return his greeting?"

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The חסיד begins answering the official's challenge from step 41.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Parable (משל) comparing standing in תפילה to standing before a king.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Ignoring the official was a reckless risk to his life.
steps.terutzMaskana: The answer is still in progress: standing before the King of kings means one cannot interrupt, just as before a human king.
